{{short description|Theorem about inclusions between Sobolev spaces}}
In [[mathematics]], there is in [[mathematical analysis]] a class of '''Sobolev inequalities''', relating norms including those of [[Sobolev space]]s. These are used to prove the '''Sobolev embedding theorem''', giving inclusions between certain [[Sobolev space]]s, and the [[Rellich–Kondrachov theorem]] showing that under slightly stronger conditions some Sobolev spaces are [[compactly embedded]] in others. They are named after [[Sergei Lvovich Sobolev]].

==Sobolev embedding theorem==

[[File:Sobolev embedding theorem.svg|thumb|250px|Graphical representation of the embedding conditions. The space {{math|''W<sup>&thinsp;3,p</sup>''}}, represented by a blue dot at the point {{math|(1/''p'', 3)}}, embeds into the spaces indicated by red dots, all lying on a line with slope {{math|''n''}}. The white circle at {{math|(0,0)}} indicates the impossibility of optimal embeddings into {{math|''L<sup>&thinsp;∞</sup>''}}.]]
Let {{math|''W<sup>&thinsp;k,p</sup>''('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>)}} denote the [[Sobolev space]] consisting of all real-valued functions on {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} whose [[weak derivative]]s up to order {{mvar|k}} are functions in {{math|[[Lp space|''L<sup>p</sup>'']]}}. Here {{mvar|k}} is a non-negative integer and {{math|1 ≤ ''p'' < ∞}}. The first part of the Sobolev embedding theorem states that if {{math|''k'' > ''ℓ''}}, {{math|''p'' < ''n''}} and {{math|1 ≤ ''p'' < ''q'' < ∞}} are two real numbers such that

:<math>\frac{1}{p}-\frac{k}{n} = \frac{1}{q} -\frac{\ell}{n},  </math>

(given <math>n</math>, <math>p</math>, <math>k</math> and <math>\ell</math> this is satisfied for some <math>q \in [1, \infty)</math> provided <math>(k- \ell) p < n </math>),
then

:<math>W^{k,p}(\mathbf{R}^n)\subseteq W^{\ell,q}(\mathbf{R}^n)</math>

and the embedding is continuous: for every <math>f \in W^{k,p}(\mathbf{R}^n)</math>, one has 
<math>f \in W^{l,q}(\mathbf{R}^n)</math>, and 

:<math>
 \biggl(\int_{\mathbf{R}^n} \vert \nabla^\ell f\vert^q \biggr)^\frac{1}{q}
\le C \biggl(\int_{\mathbf{R}^n} \vert \nabla^k f\vert^p \biggr)^\frac{1}{p}.
</math>

In the special case of {{math|''k'' {{=}} 1}} and {{math|''ℓ'' {{=}} 0}}, Sobolev embedding gives

:<math>W^{1,p}(\mathbf{R}^n) \subseteq L^{p^*}(\mathbf{R}^n)</math>

where {{math|''p''<sup>∗</sup>}} is the '''[[Sobolev conjugate]]''' of {{mvar|p}}, given by<!-- only if p<n! -->

:<math>\frac{1}{p^*} = \frac{1}{p} - \frac{1}{n}</math>
and for every <math>f \in W^{1,p}(\mathbf{R}^n)</math>, one has 
<math>f \in L^{p^*}(\mathbf{R}^n)</math> and 
:<math>
 \biggl(\int_{\mathbf{R}^n} \vert f\vert^{p^*} \biggr)^{\frac{1}{p^*}}
\le C \biggl(\int_{\mathbf{R}^n} \vert \nabla f\vert^p \biggr)^{\frac{1}{p}}.
</math>

This special case of the Sobolev embedding is a direct consequence of the [[#Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality|Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality]]. The result should be interpreted as saying that if a function <math>f</math> in <math>L^p(\mathbf{R}^n)</math> has one derivative in <math>L^p</math>, then <math>f</math> itself has improved local behavior, meaning that it belongs to the space <math>L^{p^*}</math> where <math>p^*>p</math>. (Note that <math>1/p^*<1/p</math>, so that <math>p^*>p</math>.) Thus, any local singularities in <math>f</math> must be more mild than for a typical function in <math>L^p</math>.

[[File:Sobolev embedding theorem (Morrey case).svg|thumb|250px|If the line from the picture above intersects the y-axis at ''s = r + α'', the embedding into a Hölder space {{math|''C<sup>&thinsp;r, α</sup>''}} (red) holds. White circles indicate intersection points at which ''optimal'' embeddings are not valid.]]

The second part of the Sobolev embedding theorem applies to embeddings in [[Hölder space]]s {{math|''C<sup>&thinsp;r,α</sup>''('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>)}}. If {{math|''n'' < ''pk''}} and

:<math>\frac{1}{p}-\frac{k}{n} = -\frac{r + \alpha}{n},  \mbox{ or, equivalently, } r + \alpha = k - \frac{n}{p}  </math>

with {{math|''α'' ∈ (0, 1)}} then one has the embedding

:<math>W^{k,p}(\mathbf{R}^n)\subset C^{r,\alpha}(\mathbf{R}^n).</math>

In other words, for every <math>f \in W^{k,p}(\mathbf{R}^n)</math> and <math>x, y \in \mathbf{R}^n</math>, one has <math> f \in C^r (\mathbf{R}^n)</math>, in addition,

:<math>
\vert \nabla^r f (x) - \nabla^r f (y) \vert
\le C \biggl(\int_{\mathbf{R}^n} \vert \nabla^k f \vert^p\biggr)^\frac{1}{p} \vert x - y \vert^\alpha.
</math>

This part of the Sobolev embedding is a direct consequence of [[#Morrey's inequality|Morrey's inequality]]. Intuitively, this inclusion expresses the fact that the existence of sufficiently many weak derivatives implies some continuity of the classical derivatives. If <math> \alpha = 1</math> then <math>W^{k,p}(\mathbf{R}^n)\subset C^{r,\gamma}(\mathbf{R}^n)</math> for every <math> \gamma \in (0,1)</math>.

In particular, as long as <math>pk>n</math>, the embedding criterion will hold with <math>r=0</math> and some positive value of <math>\alpha</math>. That is, for a function <math>f</math> on <math>\mathbb R^n</math>, if <math>f</math> has <math>k</math> derivatives in <math>L^p</math> and <math>pk>n</math>, then <math>f</math> will be continuous (and actually Hölder continuous with some positive exponent <math>\alpha</math>).

===Generalizations===
{{Further|Souček space}}
The Sobolev embedding theorem holds for Sobolev spaces {{math|''W<sup>&thinsp;k,p</sup>''(''M'')}} on other suitable domains {{mvar|M}}. In particular ({{harvnb|Aubin|1982|loc=Chapter 2}}; {{harvnb|Aubin|1976}}), both parts of the Sobolev embedding hold when
* {{mvar|M}} is a [[bounded set|bounded]] [[open set]] in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} with [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz]] boundary (or whose boundary satisfies the [[cone condition]]; {{harvnb|Adams|1975|loc=Theorem 5.4}})
* {{mvar|M}} is a [[compact space|compact]] [[Riemannian manifold]]
* {{mvar|M}} is a compact Riemannian [[manifold with boundary]] and the boundary is Lipschitz (meaning that the boundary can be locally represented as a graph of a Lipschitz continuous function).
* {{mvar|M}} is a [[complete manifold|complete]] Riemannian manifold with [[injectivity radius]] {{math|''δ'' > 0}} and bounded [[sectional curvature]].
If {{mvar|M}} is a bounded open set in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} with continuous boundary, then {{math|''W<sup>&thinsp;1,2</sup>''(''M'')}} is compactly embedded in {{math|''L<sup>2</sup>''(''M'')}} ({{harvnb|Nečas|2012|loc=Section 1.1.5, Theorem 1.4}}).

===Kondrachov embedding theorem===
{{main article|Rellich–Kondrachov theorem}}
On a compact manifold {{math|''M''}} with {{math|''C''<sup>1</sup>}} boundary, the '''Kondrachov embedding theorem''' states that if {{math|''k'' > ''ℓ''}} and<math display="block">\frac{1}{p}-\frac{k}{n} < \frac{1}{q} -\frac{\ell}{n}</math>then the Sobolev embedding

:<math>W^{k,p}(M)\subset W^{\ell,q}(M)</math>

is [[completely continuous]] (compact).<ref name="Taylor">{{cite book | author=Taylor, Michael E. | title=Partial Differential Equations I - Basic Theory | year=1997 | edition=2nd | isbn=0-387-94653-5 | page=286}}</ref> Note that the condition is just as in the first part of the Sobolev embedding theorem, with the equality replaced by an inequality, thus requiring a more regular space {{math|''W<sup>&thinsp;k,p</sup>''(''M'')}}.

==Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality==
Assume that {{mvar|u}} is a continuously differentiable real-valued function on {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} with [[compact support]]. Then for {{math|1 &le; ''p'' < ''n''}} there is a constant {{mvar|C}} depending only on {{mvar|n}} and {{mvar|p}} such that

: <math>\|u\|_{L^{p^*}(\mathbf{R}^n)}\leq C \|Du\|_{L^{p}(\mathbf{R}^n)}.</math>

with <math>1/p^* = 1/p - 1/n</math>.
The case <math> 1< p < n </math> is due to Sobolev<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sobolev |first1=Sergeĭ L’vovich |title=Sur un théorème de l'analyse fonctionnelle |journal=Comptes Rendus (Doklady) de l'Académie des Sciences de l'URSS |series=Nouvelle Série |date=1938 |volume=20 |pages=5–9}}</ref> and the case <math>p =1 </math> to [[Emilio Gagliardo|Gagliardo]] and [[Louis Nirenberg|Nirenberg]] independently.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gagliardo |first1=Emilio |title=Proprietà di alcune classi di funzioni in più variabili |journal=Ricerche di Matematica |date=1958 |volume=7 |pages=102–137}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nirenberg |first1=Louis |title=On elliptic partial differential equations |journal=Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa. Classe di Scienze. Serie III |date=1959 |volume=13 |pages=115–162}}</ref> The Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality implies directly the Sobolev embedding

:<math>W^{1,p}(\mathbf{R}^n) \sub L^{p^*}(\mathbf{R}^n).</math>

The embeddings in other orders on {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} are then obtained by suitable iteration.

==Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev lemma==
Sobolev's original proof of the Sobolev embedding theorem relied on the following, sometimes known as the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev [[fractional integration]] theorem. An equivalent statement is known as the '''Sobolev lemma''' in {{harv|Aubin|1982|loc=Chapter 2}}. A proof is in {{harv|Stein|1970|loc=Chapter V, §1.3}}.

Let {{math|0 < ''α'' < ''n''}} and {{math|1 < ''p'' < ''q'' < ∞}}. Let {{math|''I<sub>α</sub>'' {{=}} (−Δ)<sup>−''α''/2</sup>}} be the [[Riesz potential]] on {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}. Then, for {{mvar|q}} defined by

:<math>\frac 1 q = \frac 1 p - \frac \alpha n</math>

there exists a constant {{mvar|C}} depending only on {{mvar|p}} such that

:<math>\left \|I_\alpha f \right \|_q \le C \|f\|_p.</math>

If {{math|''p'' {{=}} 1}}, then one has two possible replacement estimates. The first is the more classical weak-type estimate:

:<math>m \left \{x : \left |I_\alpha f(x) \right | > \lambda \right \} \le C \left( \frac{\|f\|_1}{\lambda} \right )^q,</math>

where {{math|1/''q'' {{=}} 1 − ''α''/''n''}}. Alternatively one has the estimate for dimension n≥2<math display="block">\left \|I_\alpha f \right \|_q \le C \|Rf\|_1,</math>where <math> Rf </math> is the vector-valued [[Riesz transform]], cf. {{harv|Schikorra | Spector | Van Schaftingen|2017}}. The boundedness of the [[Riesz transform]]s implies that the latter inequality gives a unified way to write the family of inequalities for the Riesz potential.

The Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev lemma implies the Sobolev embedding essentially by the relationship between the [[Riesz transform]]s and the Riesz potentials.

==Morrey's inequality==
Assume {{math|''n'' < ''p'' ≤ ∞}}. Then there exists a constant {{mvar|C}}, depending only on {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|n}}, such that

:<math>\|u\|_{C^{0,\gamma}(\mathbf{R}^n)}\leq C \|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbf{R}^n)}</math>

for all {{math|''u'' ∈ ''C''<sup>1</sup>('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>) ∩ ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>)}}, where

:<math>\gamma=1-\frac{n}{p}.</math>

Thus if {{math|''u'' ∈ ''W''<sup>&thinsp;1,''p''</sup>('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>)}}, then {{mvar|u}} is in fact [[Hölder continuous]] of exponent {{mvar|γ}}, after possibly being redefined on a set of measure 0.

A similar result holds in a bounded domain {{mvar|U}} with Lipschitz boundary. In this case,

:<math>\|u\|_{C^{0,\gamma}(U)}\leq C \|u\|_{W^{1,p}(U)}</math>

where the constant {{mvar|C}} depends now on {{math|''n'', ''p''}} and {{mvar|U}}. This version of the inequality follows from the previous one by applying the norm-preserving extension of {{math|''W''<sup>&thinsp;1,''p''</sup>(''U'')}} to {{math|''W''<sup>&thinsp;1,''p''</sup>('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>)}}. The inequality is named after [[Charles B. Morrey Jr.]]

==General Sobolev inequalities==
Let {{mvar|U}} be a bounded open subset of {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, with a {{math|''C''<sup>1</sup>}} boundary. ({{mvar|U}} may also be unbounded, but in this case its boundary, if it exists, must be sufficiently well-behaved.)

Assume {{math|''u'' ∈ ''W<sup>&thinsp;k,p</sup>''(''U'')}}. Then we consider two cases:

==={{math|''k'' < ''n''/''p''}} or {{math|''k'' {{=}} ''n''}}, {{math|''p'' {{=}} 1}}===
In this case we conclude that {{math|''u'' ∈ ''L<sup>q</sup>''(''U'')}}, where

:<math>\frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{p}-\frac{k}{n}.</math>

We have in addition the estimate

:<math>\|u\|_{L^q(U)}\leq C \|u\|_{W^{k,p}(U)}</math>,

the constant {{mvar|C}} depending only on {{math|''k'', ''p'', ''n''}}, and {{mvar|U}}.

==={{math|''k'' > ''n''/''p''}}===
Here, we conclude that {{mvar|u}} belongs to a [[Hölder space]], more precisely:

:<math> u \in C^{k-\left[\frac{n}{p}\right]-1,\gamma}(U),</math>

where

:<math>\gamma = \begin{cases}
\left[\frac{n}{p}\right]+1-\frac{n}{p} & \frac{n}{p} \notin \mathbf{Z} \\
\text{any element in } (0, 1) & \frac{n}{p} \in \mathbf{Z}
\end{cases}</math>

We have in addition the estimate

:<math>\|u\|_{C^{k-\left[\frac{n}{p}\right]-1,\gamma}(U)}\leq C \|u\|_{W^{k,p}(U)},</math>

the constant {{mvar|C}} depending only on {{math|''k'', ''p'', ''n'', ''γ''}}, and {{mvar|U}}. In particular, the condition <math>k>n/p</math> guarantees that <math>u</math> is continuous (and actually Hölder continuous with some positive exponent).

==Case {{math|1=''p''=''n'', ''k''=1}}==
If <math>u\in W^{1,n}(\mathbf{R}^n)</math>, then {{mvar|u}} is a function of [[bounded mean oscillation]] and

:<math>|u|_{\operatorname{BMO}(\mathbf R^n)} \leq C \|Du\|_{L^n(\mathbf{R}^n)},</math>

for some constant {{mvar|C}} depending only on {{mvar|n}}.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brezis |first1=H. |last2=Nirenberg |first2=L. |title=Degree theory and BMO; part I: Compact manifolds without boundaries |journal=Selecta Mathematica |date=September 1995 |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=197–263 |doi=10.1007/BF01671566|s2cid=195270732 }}</ref>{{rp|§I.2}} This estimate is a corollary of the [[Poincaré inequality]]. (It should as well be stressed that on the left hand side is the BMO ''semi''norm.)

==Case {{math|1=''kp''=''n''}}==
The prior result may be extended to arbitrary degree <math>k</math> <ref>{{cite book|last=Leoni |first=Giovanni |date=2017 |title="A First Course in Sobolev Spaces" (2nd Ed) |publisher=American Mathematical Society |page=373}}</ref>{{rp|§12.2}}. For <math>k\geq 2</math>, if <math>kp=n</math>, then for every <math>u\in W^{k,n/k}(\mathbf R^n)</math> there exists a polynomial <math>P</math> of degree <math>k-1</math> such that 

:<math> \Vert u-P\circ u\Vert_{\operatorname{BMO}(\mathbf R^n)}\leq C\Vert D^k u\Vert_{L^{n/k}(\mathbf R^n)}</math>

additionally, for any <math> j=1,\dots,k-1</math>, we have

:<math> \Vert D^j(u-P\circ u)\Vert_{L^{n/j}(\mathbf R^n)}\leq C \Vert D^k u\Vert_{L^{n/k}(\mathbf R^n)} </math>

In particular this implies the inclusion embedding

:<math> W^{k,n/k}(\mathbf R^n) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{BMO}(\mathbf R^n)\cap W^{1,q_1}(\mathbf R^n)\cap \dots\cap W^{k-1,q_{k-1}}(\mathbf R^n) </math>

for all exponents <math>q_j</math> satisfying <math>n/k\leq q_j\leq n/j</math>, <math>j=1,\dots,k-1</math>.

==Nash inequality==
The Nash inequality, introduced by {{harvs|first=John|last=Nash|authorlink=John Forbes Nash, Jr.|year=1958|txt}}, states that there exists a constant {{math|''C'' > 0}}, such that for all {{math|''u'' ∈ ''L''<sup>1</sup>('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>) ∩ ''W''<sup>&thinsp;1,2</sup>('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>)}},

:<math>\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbf{R}^n)}^{1+2/n} \leq C\|u\|_{L^1(\mathbf{R}^n)}^{2/n} \| Du\|_{L^2(\mathbf{R}^n)}.</math>

The inequality follows from basic properties of the [[Fourier transform]]. Indeed, integrating over the complement of the ball of radius {{mvar|ρ}},

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\int_{|x|\ge\rho} \left |\hat{u}(x) \right |^2\,dx \le \int_{|x|\ge\rho} \frac{|x|^2}{\rho^2} \left |\hat{u}(x) \right |^2\,dx\le \rho^{-2}\int_{\mathbf{R}^n}|D u|^2\,dx</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

because <math>1\le|x|^2/\rho^2</math>. On the other hand, one has

:<math>|\hat{u}| \le \|u\|_{L^1}</math>

which, when integrated over the ball of radius {{mvar|ρ}} gives

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\int_{|x|\le\rho} |\hat{u}(x)|^2\,dx \le \rho^n\omega_n \|u\|_{L^1}^2</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

where {{math|''ω<sub>n</sub>''}} is the volume of the [[n sphere|{{mvar|n}}-ball]]. Choosing {{mvar|ρ}} to minimize the sum of ({{EquationNote|1}}) and ({{EquationNote|2}}) and applying Parseval's theorem:

:<math>\|\hat{u}\|_{L^2} = \|u\|_{L^2}</math>

gives the inequality.

In the special case of {{math|''n'' {{=}} 1}}, the Nash inequality can be extended to the {{math|''L<sup>p</sup>''}} case, in which case it is a generalization of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Sobolev inequality ({{harvnb|Brezis|2011}}, Comments on Chapter 8). In fact, if {{mvar|I}} is a bounded interval, then for all {{math|1 ≤ ''r'' < ∞}} and all {{math|1 ≤ ''q'' ≤ ''p'' < ∞}} the following inequality holds

:<math>\| u\|_{L^p(I)}\le C\| u\|^{1-a}_{L^q(I)} \|u\|^a_{W^{1,r}(I)},</math>

where:

:<math>a\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{r}+1\right)=\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{p}.</math>

==Logarithmic Sobolev inequality==

{{main|Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities}}

The simplest of the Sobolev embedding theorems, described above, states that if a function <math>f</math> in <math>L^p(\mathbb R^n)</math> has one derivative in <math>L^p</math>, then <math>f</math> itself is in <math>L^{p^*}</math>, where

:<math>1/p^*=1/p-1/n.</math>

We can see that as <math>n</math> tends to infinity, <math>p^*</math> approaches <math>p</math>. Thus, if the dimension <math>n</math> of the space on which <math>f</math> is defined is large, the improvement in the local behavior of <math>f</math> from having a derivative in <math>L^p</math> is small (<math>p^*</math> is only slightly larger than <math>p</math>). In particular, for functions on an infinite-dimensional space, we cannot expect any direct analog of the classical Sobolev embedding theorems.

There is, however, a type of Sobolev inequality, established by [[Leonard Gross]] ({{harvnb|Gross|1975}}) and known as a [[logarithmic Sobolev inequalities|logarithmic Sobolev inequality]], that has dimension-independent constants and therefore continues to hold in the infinite-dimensional setting. The logarithmic Sobolev inequality says, roughly, that if a function is in <math>L^p</math> with respect to a Gaussian measure and has one derivative that is also in <math>L^p</math>, then <math>f</math> is in "<math>L^p</math>-log", meaning that the integral of <math>|f|^p\log|f|</math> is finite. The inequality expressing this fact has constants that do not involve the dimension of the space and, thus, the inequality holds in the setting of a Gaussian measure on an infinite-dimensional space. It is now known that logarithmic Sobolev inequalities hold for many different types of measures, not just Gaussian measures.

Although it might seem as if the <math>L^p</math>-log condition is a very small improvement over being in <math>L^p</math>, this improvement is sufficient to derive an important result, namely hypercontractivity for the associated [[Dirichlet form]] operator. This result means that if a function is in the range of the exponential of the Dirichlet form operator—which means that the function has, in some sense, infinitely many derivatives in <math>L^p</math>—then the function does belong to <math>L^{p^*}</math> for some <math>p^*>p</math> ({{harvnb|Gross|1975}} Theorem 6).
